title: Seven People, One Hectare and Hand-Dug Wells at Porto-Novo
dek: In 1985 a Nigerian-born priest began farming a scrap of abandoned land in Benin, and it grew into a training centre for young farmers.

story.event: Starting an integrated farm and training centre on barely a hectare of abandoned land in Porto-Novo
story.summary: In 1985 Godfrey Nzamujo, a Nigerian-born Dominican priest who had studied in the United States, began the Songhai Centre on barely a hectare of abandoned land in Porto-Novo given by Benin's then-Marxist government, with six others digging wells and watering by hand. Built on recycling farm waste instead of chemicals, it grew to about 24 hectares by 2014, training some 400 apprentices a year.
paragraphs: In 1985 Godfrey Nzamujo and six others began work on a plot of barely a hectare at Porto-Novo, the capital of Benin. "It was abandoned land, killed by chemical fertiliser and conventional agricultural practices," he later told the news agency AFP. "There were seven of us. We dug wells and watered with our own hands."

Nzamujo, a Nigerian-born Dominican priest who had studied in the United States and lived in California, said he had been shocked at the start of the 1980s by television pictures of famine in Africa. He set out to see where his training in agronomy, economics and computing could be of use. After visiting several countries he settled in Benin, whose then-Marxist government gave him the small plot.

His method was to copy nature, where, as he told Jeune Afrique, everything is transformed. In time Songhai used compost from its own plant waste instead of chemical fertiliser, encouraged the soil's bacteria, ran water through ponds of water hyacinth before it reached the fish, and turned chicken droppings and spent hyacinths into biogas for the kitchens. The aim, the magazine wrote, was to show that a little ingenuity could produce plenty on small plots. At first, Nzamujo said, the centre was meant to train young rural people and give them the means to support themselves.

In the main dry season, he recalled, the grey ground turned green. By 2014 the Porto-Novo centre covered 24 hectares, and by Songhai's account its rice yield had risen from one tonne per hectare once a year to seven tonnes three times a year. About 400 apprentices, chosen by competition, took a free 18-month course each year before going out to villages, where the centre kept checking on them. Jeune Afrique reported sales across Songhai's farms of 7 billion CFA francs in 2013. When the FAO gave Nzamujo a medal in 2015, he said it was not a crowning achievement but an encouragement to work harder.

quote.text: 'And when they have been enriched, what more shall be done?' The Master said, 'Teach them.'
quote.source_title: The Analects of Confucius (from the Chinese Classics), tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #3330
quote.connection: Seeing the crowds of Wei, Confucius said the first task was to enrich the people; asked what came next, he answered in two words. Songhai kept that order: dead land had to produce before the farm could become a school.

reflection: Nzamujo did not begin with 24 hectares, a shop or visiting heads of state. He began with ground other people had given up on, seven pairs of hands and a long wait for the first green.

Much of what you are building may still be at the well-digging stage, where the work is heavy and little shows above ground. The old order in the quote is a kind thing to remember on a tired day: first make something that feeds people, then teach others to do it. Neither has to be finished this year.
invitation: Choose one patch of your work that is still bare ground. Give it one unglamorous hour today, the equivalent of carrying water, and stop when the hour is up.

sources.title: Organic farm in Benin looks to set example for Africa (Cecile De Comarmond, AFP)
sources.supports: Songhai started in 1985 in Porto-Novo on barely a hectare; Benin's then-Marxist government gave Nzamujo a small plot of abandoned land; his quotations 'It was abandoned land, killed by chemical fertiliser and conventional agricultural practices' and 'There were seven of us. We dug wells and watered with our own hands'; famine images on television in the early 1980s; the 'nothing is wasted, everything is transformed' principle; biogas from chicken droppings; water hyacinth filtering; no pesticides or fertilisers; 24 hectares by 2014; rice from one tonne per hectare once a year to seven tonnes three times a year; about 400 apprentices a year chosen by competition on a free 18-month course, then sent to villages and checked.

sources.title: Organic farm in Benin looks to set example for Africa (AFP; fuller text of the same report)
sources.supports: Nzamujo, Nigeria-born and raised in California, shocked by famine images at the start of the 1980s, left to see how to use his training in agronomics, economics and information technology; after visiting several countries he ended up in Benin; 'during the main dry season, this grey surface became green'.

sources.title: Bénin : la petite ferme modèle
sources.supports: Songhai created in 1985 by the Dominican priest; aim to prove that with a little ingenuity and goodwill one can produce plenty on small surfaces; Nzamujo on applying nature's principle that everything is transformed; compost from plant waste; water through hyacinth ponds to the fish ponds; spent hyacinths and poultry droppings made into biogas for the kitchens; at first the centre was to train young rural people and give them the means to support themselves; declared a UN centre of excellence for agriculture.

sources.title: Fermes agricoles : une réussite nommée Songhaï (Réussite)
sources.supports: Nzamujo, a microbiologist and engineer of Nigerian origin, left California thirty years earlier to found the first Songhai centre in Porto-Novo; 17 Songhai farms in Benin, Nigeria, Sierra Leone and Liberia; 7 billion CFA francs of sales and 600 million profit in 2013; a 25-hectare model farm.

sources.title: Agro-tourism essential for Africans to know latest on agric wealth creation (interview by Oluyinka Alawode)
sources.supports: Nzamujo is a Dominican priest and founder-director of the Songhai Centre in Porto-Novo, started in 1985; integrated model in which livestock waste fertilises crops and crops feed animals; about 3,500 trained by 2014.

sources.title: Godfrey Nzamujo, fondateur du Centre Songhaï, distingué pour son action en faveur de la lutte contre la faim et la pauvreté au Bénin
sources.supports: FAO 70th-anniversary medal presented to Nzamujo on 15 December 2015; his remark that the medal was not a consecration but an encouragement to redouble efforts; originally from Nigeria and trained in the United States; dates the Songhai model's founding to 1984.

cross_checks.claim: Nzamujo started the Songhai Centre in Porto-Novo, Benin, in 1985.
Nzamujo was a Nigerian-born priest who had trained in the United States and came from California.
Songhai's method recycles farm waste (compost, water hyacinth ponds, biogas from droppings) in place of chemical inputs.
The centre was set up to train young people in farming.

research_notes: Founding year: AFP (2014), Jeune Afrique (2013) and BusinessDay (2014) give 1985; the UN in Benin's 2015 note gives 1984. The story uses 1985. The one-hectare start, the land's condition, the government's gift and the seven people digging wells rest on Nzamujo's own account to AFP (2014), published in full by FreshPlaza and in a shorter version by Phys.org; they are the same report, not independent of each other. A 2025 AllAfrica interview (blocked to automated requests, so not cited) is described in search results as also giving a one-hectare start on a ruined government farm. Background: AFP says he was raised in California; Jeune Afrique calls him an engineer of Nigerian origin who left California; the UN says he was trained in the United States; the story says he 'had studied in the United States and lived in California'. Area by 2014-15: 24 hectares (AFP) or 25 (Jeune Afrique 2015); the story uses AFP's. Training numbers differ by source and date (AFP: about 400 apprentices a year; BusinessDay 2014: about 3,500 trained in all); the story uses AFP's annual figure. The rice-yield figures are Songhai's own, reported by AFP, and are attributed. The 7 billion CFA figure is Jeune Afrique's for all Songhai farms in 2013. The recycling methods are described as they were in 2013-14 ('in time'), not as the 1985 practice. Jeune Afrique quotations are in French and are paraphrased, not quoted; the FAO-medal remark is paraphrased from the UN's French text. Funding is set to 'mixed': the land came from the state, the centre later earned revenue from its own sales, and the UN describes support from the government, partners and UN agencies for its expansion; none of the cited sources documents how the 1985 start was financed. Quote: the Analects passage is the end of Book XIII, Chapter 9, in which Confucius, driving through Wei with Zan Yu, says the numerous people should first be enriched; the excerpt begins at section 4 so as not to splice across Legge's section numbers. The company field is 'Songhai' rather than the slate's 'Songhai Centre', because the repeat screen matched the word 'Centre' with an unrelated organisation (Tilganga, in the Sanduk Ruit edition).
